title: Receptive-field size across the body
objective: Explain two-point discrimination differences and preview sparse visceral fields.

steps.title: Why fingertips beat your back
steps.body: **[[two-point discrimination]]** — the smallest gap you can feel as *two* points — is tiny on the fingertip (dense small fields) and large on the back (sparse big fields). Same skin, different receptive-field grids.

steps.prompt: Two points feel like one on the back but clearly two on the fingertip. Why?
options: The back has larger, sparser receptive fields
The back's afferents are mostly slow C fibers
The back sits closer to the spinal cord itself
steps.explanation: Acuity follows receptive-field density. Sparse, large fields on the back merge nearby points; dense, small fields on the fingertip resolve them.

variants.setup: You test two-point discrimination on fingertip vs back.
variants.prompt: Where is the threshold gap smaller?
variants.reveal: Dense small fields on the fingertip resolve closer points, so its threshold is smaller.

steps.setup: An organ like the colon is innervated by relatively few, widely-branching afferents.
steps.prompt: What do you predict about localizing a stimulus there?
options: Precise, but only for painful stimuli
steps.reveal: Sparse afferents with large fields mean the brain gets 'something's happening in there' but not precisely where — the heart of why visceral sensation is diffuse (unit D5).

variants.prompt: Sparse, large-field innervation of an organ gives…
variants.explanation: Few neurons with big fields can't localize precisely, giving diffuse sensation.

steps.title: Skin vs viscera
steps.body: Skin is densely mapped for acuity; the viscera are sparsely innervated for *detecting* events (stretch, injury, chemistry), not for pinpointing them. That design choice is exactly what the next unit unpacks.

sources.note: DRG afferents sensing distal-colon mechanics; visceral stretch sensation.
